text.en: After visiting the Mauryan empire, Bhavisha and Dhruv are ready for another adventure. Very little is known about Ashoka's successors. The great empire shrank and the northwest was weakened. What happened next? New kingdoms arose in many places, some foreign rulers settled and became part of India, and art and ideas mixed. This is the age of reorganisation.

After Ashoka the empire declined. The northwest became weak, exposing the subcontinent to invasions from outside, while regional powers rose to claim land. This period saw the revival of Vedic rituals, but other schools of thought, Buddhist and Jain, flourished too. Sanskrit became one of the preferred languages for philosophical and literary works.
The Shunga dynasty ruled in central India. The Bharhut Stupa in Madhya Pradesh has beautiful Shunga art, including panels and a female figure with hair ornaments in terracotta. The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan. Trade flourished, and a Satavahana coin shows a sea-going ship with two masts. Agriculture thrived in the Krishna-Godavari region. Satavahana kings often granted tax-free farm land to Vedic scholars and Buddhist and Jain monks. A powerful queen donated land to monks and had an important inscription carved in Nashik, listing gifts of land, cows, horses, elephants and silver coins.
In Kalinga, a ruler took pride in protecting all schools of thought. Near Bhubaneswar the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves, probably made for Jain monks, show intricate panels, statues and spacious rooms carved in rock, showing the skill of the craftsmen.
In the south the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas rose. The Sangam literature, the oldest in south India, is a collection of poems and is consulted by historians for society and culture. The Chola king Karikala is said to have defeated a combined force of the Cheras and Pandyas. He is credited with building embankments along the Kaveri to divert water to the delta, which helped farming. The Cheras traded with the Roman Empire and West Asia, exporting Indian goods, and issued coins. The Pandyas were a naval power and wrote in inscriptions about their care for their subjects and their encouragement of all schools of thought. In the epic Silappadikaram, Kannagi gives her husband Kovalan an anklet to sell, but he is falsely accused of theft and executed by the Pandya king. She walks to the Chera kingdom and is honoured as a goddess.
The Indo-Greeks, who came after Alexander, left a blend of Greek and Indian elements in governance, art, language and life. Some coins show Indian deities like Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi, and the Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha shows a Greek ambassador adopting Indian devotion. The Kushanas, from Central Asia, entered India in about the 2nd century CE. Their art, the Gandhara and Mathura schools, is famous for a fusion of Indian and Greek styles. Gandhara used grey-black schist stone, while Mathura used red sandstone with less Greco-Roman influence. Coins of their emperors show Shiva with the bull Nandi on the other side. This is how foreign invaders assimilated into Indian society and contributed to a cultural confluence.
Dates in some official publications are given in both the Gregorian and Shaka Samvat eras. The Shaka calendar was adopted as the Indian National Calendar in 1957. It was also an age when Sanskrit literature flourished, including major texts like the Mahabharata and Ramayana taking their final form, which leads towards the Gupta era.

problem.en: Identify which school of art: grey-black schist with Greek-style folds, or red sandstone figures.

text.en: Grey-black schist with Greco-Roman influence is Gandhara.
Red sandstone with less Greek influence is Mathura.
Both belong to the Kushana period.

prompt.en: How did foreign rulers become part of Indian culture?

requiredIdeas.en: They used Indian deities on coins.
They patronised Buddhism and local art.
They mixed Greek and Indian styles in art.

points.en: After the Mauryas, many regional kingdoms rose.
Satavahanas, Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas flourished in the south.
Indo-Greeks and Kushanas blended with Indian culture; Gandhara and Mathura art grew.
Sangam literature is the oldest in south India.
